title: The king with the broom
hookLine: sandalwood water on a swept road: a king picks up a broom in front of the chariot
carry: bhakti's highest rank: servant of the servants
tomorrow: this life story ends at night, in tears. why end there?

cards: Sandalwood has a smell that hangs in the air: warm, woody, a little sweet. In this scene it's on a road.
The great chariot of Jagannatha is about to roll through Puri, the crowd is packed in, and the king steps out in front of it.
Prataparudra, ruler of the land, takes a broom, sweeps the road clean, and sprinkles it with sandalwood water, like a servant of the temple. Why would a king do that?

teach.h: THE KING ASKS, AND IS REFUSED.
teach.b: Prataparudra has been asking to meet Chaitanya, and Chaitanya keeps saying no: in the book, he holds that a renunciant shouldn't seek out the company of kings. Friends plead. He doesn't move.
So the king stops asking for an audience and starts serving.
He sweeps. Chaitanya, singing nearby, sees it, and the Charitamrita says he was pleased. Then a second scene.
After the dancing, Chaitanya rests in a garden. The king comes alone, not in royal dress but in a devotee's simple clothes.
He presses Chaitanya's feet and begins reciting from the Bhagavata: the gopis' song of longing for Krishna, with its line that the nectar of Krishna's words gives life to those who burn.
Chaitanya, hearing it, cries out for more, then rises and embraces him. Only afterward does he ask: who are you? The king answers: the servant of your servants.
So that's why a king picks up a broom. No title, no gift, no clever argument opened the door.

teach.h: A VERSE SUNG IN A GARDEN.
teach.b: A broom, the smell of sandalwood on a swept road, and a verse sung with love.
In this book, bhakti comes in by the servant's entrance. Gaudiya Vaishnavas take the king's answer as their ideal: to be the servant of the servants of Krishna.
And at every Ratha Yatra in Puri, the king of Puri still sweeps the chariots before they roll, a rite called chhera pahara.

how: At the Ratha Yatra in Puri, the chariot festival of Jagannatha, the king of Puri sweeps the chariots before they roll, a rite called chhera pahara; devotees tell Prataparudra's story as a picture of service before rank.

games.q: watching the Ratha Yatra with Nani, your little cousin sees the king of Puri sweeping the chariot and asks why a king is cleaning. what do you tell her?
o: in bhakti, the best title is servant of the Lord's servants, so sweeping for Jagannatha is an honor.
it's just for the cameras; kings don't really sweep.
the temple sweepers must have had the day off.
games.why: Prataparudra swept the road before the chariot and called himself the servant of your servants. the king of Puri still sweeps the chariots each Ratha Yatra, a rite called chhera pahara.

practice: If you have a home shrine or altar, slowly wipe it with a cloth: the edge, the base, the space around the images. If not, wipe any one small surface near you. Notice the sound and any smell in the air.
Do it the way the king swept, as service, as if this little road mattered.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti, in a king's hands: a broom, sandalwood water, and the servant's entrance.

orig.note: Sanskrit chandana, sandalwood; in this story, the sandalwood water the king sprinkles on the swept road.

carryVoice: Keep this: bhakti's highest rank is servant of the servants. A king with a broom said so. One more day of the book.

sources.ref: Chaitanya Charitamrita, Madhya-lila 11 (Chaitanya refuses to meet King Prataparudra: a renunciant should not seek the company of kings)
